newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Police shoot Irish guerrilla after robbery.
newsitem.headline: Police shoot Irish guerrilla after robbery.

text.p: A raider shot dead by Irish police after an armed robbery was a member of the outlawed Irish National Liberation Army (INLA) guerrilla group, the INLA said on Thursday.
In a statement issued to media in Belfast, capital of British Northern Ireland, the INLA named him as John Morris and decribed him as "a volunteer of our South Dublin Brigade".

Police said Morris died in hospital after being wounded on Wednesday by an officer who had been called to a robbery at premises of a newspaper distribution firm at an industrial factory zone. Two other men were arrested.
"They were confronted by armed gardai (police) who had been alerted to the situation," a police spokesman said.
"During the course of the confrontation one raider was shot. Money, a firearm and a knife were recovered at the scene."
The INLA, a small left-wing guerrilla group opposed to British rule in Northern Ireland, said Morris's gun was not loaded and that he had not offered resistance.
"This was no more than a state execution of a known Republican Socialist. It will not be forgotten." Irish police said the incident was being investigated.
The INLA, whose power base is in Belfast, shot dead an off-duty police officer in a crowded bar in Belfast last month.
A small organisation with a bloody history, it has been riven by internal power struggles that triggered vicious feuds over recent years.
The Belfast killing was its first attack for several years on a member of the British security forces.
The INLA was dormant during a 17 month truce observed by the main guerrilla organisation, the Irish Republican Army, until February last year.
Ireland has seen little of the guerrilla activity that has killed 3,200 in the conflict over Northern Ireland but the IRA and its offshoots are illegal organisations under Irish law.
The nation was angered last year when IRA activists shot dead a policeman in a bungled post office robbery in the southern town of Adare.
It turned many IRA sympathisers into informers and led to a spate of guerrilla arms caches being uncovered, security sources said.
